cells.quote: A lower level of PICC maintenance knowledge was noted for nurses under 25 years of age (B=−0.054, p<0.05), those with a professional title of nurse (B=−0.074, p<0.01), those working in county hospitals (B=−0.028, p<0.01) and those who had not received PICC maintenance training previously (B=−0.075, p<0.01) compared with the nurses aged 45 years old or above, those with a professional title of cochief nurse, those working in provincial hospitals and those who had received PICC maintenance training before, respectively (table 5).
cells.note: Professional title is a measured learner characteristic; the cross-sectional design does not establish causation.

cells.quote: Following the training, participants’ total knowledge scores improved by five percentage points to 82.6 ± 11.0% (t-value = 7.119, p < 0.001; see Table 2).
cells.note: Paired pre/post assessment; no randomization or separate control group.

D.treatment: interactive hypoglycemia training with practical demonstrations

cells.quote: For the four–question hypoglycemia test, participants averaged 55.7 ± 24.8% pre-training and 83.0 ± 22.4% post-training (mean improvement = 27.26, t-value = 14.258, p < 0.001; see Tables 2 and 3).
cells.note: Paired pre/post assessment; the study reports a very large effect.

O.outcome_detail: Diabetes attitudes across five DAS-3 subscales

cells.quote: Following the training, we observed positive improvements in diabetes attitudes for all five subscales (see Table 4): “Need for special training” (mean improvement = 0.12, t-value = 4.166, p < 0.001, n = 212); “Seriousness of type 2 diabetes” (mean improvement = 0.12, t-value = 3.647, p < 0.001); “Value of tight glucose control” (mean improvement = 0.11, t-value = 3.373, p = 0.001); “Psychosocial impact of diabetes” (mean improvement = 0.27, t-value = 9.249, p < 0.001); and “Attitude toward patient autonomy” (mean improvement = 0.17, t-value = 6.261, p < 0.001).
cells.note: Paired pre/post assessment; the reported effect-size range spans the five subscales.

D.treatment: glucagon administration demonstration and group practice

cells.quote: Lastly, participants scored 87.6 ± 18.5% on the five-question glucagon test after the training session; this was the highest average score out of all of the knowledge tests (see Tables 2 and 3).
cells.note: The five glucagon questions were deliberately omitted from the pre-assessment, so the study provides no treatment-versus-comparison contrast or effect estimate for this outcome.

O.outcome_detail: Good clinical evaluation: grade 8 or higher in at least three of five clerkships

result.effect: Wald χ 2 (1) = 78.45, p < 0.01; 62.7% broadly sampled versus 82.5% global

cells.quote: Assessment significantly predicted good clinical evaluation, implying that higher clinical evaluations were received in the global assessment (675 evaluations, 82.5%) as compared with the broadly sampled assessment (532 evaluations, 62.7%) (Wald χ 2 (1) = 78.45, p< 0.01).

result.effect: Ethnicity × assessment interaction: Wald χ 2 (4) = 15.77, p < 0.01; adjusted ORs for good evaluation in broad versus global: native Dutch 0.65, Surinamese/Antillean 0.51, Asian 0.30

cells.quote: Research question 1: ethnicity‐related differences in clinical grades were smaller in broadly sampled than in global assessment, and this was also seen after adjustments. More specifically, native Dutch students had reduced probabilities (0.87–0.65) in broadly sampled as compared with global assessment, whereas Surinamese (0.03–0.51) and Asian students (0.21–0.30) had increased probabilities of having ≥3 times a grade of 8 or higher in five clerkships.

D.treatment: supervisor deviation from algorithm-derived broadly sampled score

O.outcome_detail: Ethnicity-related differences in clinical grades and grade-point upgrades

result.effect: Unadjusted F(4) = 2.38, p = 0.05; Turkish/Moroccan/African β = −0.43, p = 0.02; effects were no longer significant after adjustment

cells.quote: Research question 2: when supervisors were allowed to deviate from original grades, ethnicity‐related differences in clinical grades were reintroduced.
cells.note: The study reports significant unadjusted ethnic differences in upgrades, but these effects were no longer significant after adjustment.

cells.quote: There was no difference in mean scores on the CanMEDS constructs of the quiz between those who completed the PDF articles and those who completed the e-learning modules (see Table 3).
cells.note: The study reports no statistically significant difference between approaches and notes that statistical power was insufficient to detect small differences; therefore direction is coded ns, not 0.

D.treatment: post-intervention assessment after either learning approach

O.outcome_detail: pooled 30-item global health knowledge quiz score

cells.quote: Overall there was an increase in conceptual knowledge in both groups with a change from the pre-test (M = 23.19/30, SD = 2.87) to the post-test (M = 24.15/30, SD = 2.94), t(58) = −2.36, p < 0.05 (two-tailed).
cells.note: The text reports a significant pooled pre-post gain but does not print a standardized effect size.
